Job 20:4.rationale: "From antiquity" refers to past time since man was placed on earth, mere antiquity rather than eternity.

2Ki 19:25.rationale: "Days of old" (qedem) refers to God's long-ago planning, mere antiquity, not a statement that anything is eternal.

Lk 10:25.rationale: The lawyer asks how to inherit "eternal life"; Jesus affirms the answer with "do this and you will live" (v. 28), treating it as life God gives.

Dt 12:19.rationale: "All your days" in the land is a lifetime duration, not a claim that anything is eternal.

Dt 12:28.rationale: Hebrew 'ad-olam: blessing ("go well with you and your children") promised forever to the obedient. BSB renders it "always," so inclusion is somewhat marginal.

Ps 55:22.rationale: God will never ('le'olam') let the righteous be shaken, a lasting promise of security to the righteous.

Job 14:20.rationale: Lanetsach here means God prevails decisively or utterly over man at death; it describes finality of human mortality, not anything called eternal or enduring forever.

Ecc 1:4.rationale: The earth is said to remain forever (le'olam), contrasted with passing human generations.

Ecc 1:10.rationale: Here 'olam means the ages before us, expressing mere antiquity rather than eternity.

Mt 24:3.rationale: "End of the age" (aiōn) refers to the close of a period, not something called eternal or lasting forever.

Mt 24:35.rationale: Jesus says his words will never pass away, unlike heaven and earth; his word is declared everlasting.

Ex 28:29.rationale: Tamid here means 'regularly/whenever he enters', a continual reminder during ministry, not a claim of eternity.

Ex 28:30.rationale: 'Continually' describes habitual practice whenever Aaron comes before the LORD, not everlasting duration.

Ex 28:38.rationale: 'Always on his forehead' means regularly while ministering; ordinary continuity, not eternity.

Ex 28:43.rationale: The priestly undergarment requirement is called a 'permanent statute' (chuqqat olam) for Aaron and his descendants.

Lev 17:7.rationale: The command to bring sacrifices only to the Tent of Meeting, not to goat demons, is called a permanent statute (chuqqat olam) for generations to come.

Ps 148:6.rationale: The heavens, sun, moon, stars and waters (vv. 3–4) are established forever by a decree that will never pass away.

Ps 37:18.rationale: The inheritance of the blameless is said to last forever (le'olam).

Ps 37:26.rationale: "Ever generous" renders kol-hayyom, "all the day", describing habitual generosity, not eternity.

Ps 37:27.rationale: Those who do good will dwell (in the land) forever; context of v. 29 suggests lasting dwelling rather than endless life as such.

Ps 37:28.rationale: God's saints are preserved forever, a lasting security promised to the righteous.

Ps 37:29.rationale: The righteous will inherit the land and dwell in it forever (la'ad).

Ecc 2:16.rationale: The verse denies any lasting (le‘olam) remembrance of the wise or the fool. It concerns human memory and is included as a negated 'forever' about human matters.

Jer 6:7.rationale: 'Ever before Me' (tamid) means continually present, describing ongoing sin, not anything called eternal.

Jer 6:16.rationale: 'Ancient paths' (netivot olam) denotes old, long-established ways, expressing antiquity rather than eternity; some might read as enduring ways of God.

Ps 41:12.rationale: God sets the psalmist, upheld in integrity, in his presence forever—a lasting blessing of dwelling with God for the righteous.

Ps 41:13.rationale: The LORD is blessed 'from everlasting to everlasting', a doxology closing Book I that ascribes eternal blessedness to God himself.
Ps 41:13.note: doxology closing Book I of Psalms

Mic 7:14.rationale: "Days of old" (olam) refers to past antiquity of Israel's history, not eternity.

Mic 7:18.rationale: Explicitly denies that God retains his anger forever, because he delights in steadfast love.

Mic 7:20.rationale: "Days of old" (qedem) denotes the ancient time of the oath to the fathers, mere antiquity rather than eternity.

2Sa 19:13.rationale: "From now on" (kol-hayyamim, 'all the days') merely sets Amasa's command going forward; nothing is called eternal or everlasting.

Jer 20:11.rationale: Jeremiah's persecutors will suffer 'an everlasting disgrace that will never be forgotten,' a judgment described as perpetual.

Jer 20:17.rationale: 'Forever' applies loosely to his mother's womb remaining pregnant, a hyperbolic lament within a curse on his birth, not a theological claim.

2Ch 18:7.rationale: Hebrew kol-yamaw ('all his days', rendered 'never') describes Micaiah's habitual prophesying, not anything eternal or everlasting.

Mk 16:8.rationale: The match comes from the 'shorter ending' appended to 16:8 in some manuscripts, which calls the gospel 'the sacred and imperishable proclamation of eternal salvation'; BSB's main text lacks it.
Mk 16:8.note: shorter ending of Mark; see BSB footnote

Jude 1:6.rationale: Rebellious angels are kept in 'eternal chains' (aidios) under darkness awaiting judgment.

Jude 1:7.rationale: Sodom and Gomorrah undergo the punishment of eternal fire as an example.

Jude 1:13.rationale: Blackest darkness is reserved forever for the false teachers.

Jude 1:21.rationale: Believers await Christ's mercy bringing them eternal life.

Jude 1:25.rationale: Doxology ascribes glory, majesty, dominion and authority to God before all time and for all ages.

Heb 9:12.rationale: Christ's self-offering secures "eternal redemption", a redemption God gives that is called eternal.

Heb 9:14.rationale: "Eternal Spirit" most naturally refers to the Holy Spirit (cf. 9:8), though some read it as Christ's own spirit; the Spirit reading is better supported.
Heb 9:14.note: some read as Christ's own spirit

Heb 9:15.rationale: Those called receive the promised "eternal inheritance", a lasting blessing for God's people.

Heb 9:26.rationale: "End of the ages" marks the eschatological time of Christ's appearing, not anything called eternal.

1Co 1:20.rationale: "This age" (aiōn) denotes the present world era, not eternity; nothing is called everlasting here.

2Ki 21:7.rationale: God declares he will establish his Name forever in the temple and in chosen Jerusalem, quoted against Manasseh's desecration.

Heb 1:2.rationale: Here aiōnas means 'the ages/universe' as created by the Son, not a statement that anything is eternal.

Heb 1:8.rationale: Addressed explicitly to the Son: his throne endures forever and ever.

Heb 1:12.rationale: In context applied to the Son as Lord and creator: he remains the same, and his years will never end.

2Ch 21:7.rationale: God promised to maintain a lamp for David and his descendants forever, grounded in the covenant made with David.

Eze 25:4.rationale: Qedem here means the East (people of the East), a direction, not eternity.

Eze 25:10.rationale: Qedem again denotes the people of the East, a direction; 'no longer remembered' is not framed as forever.

Eze 25:15.rationale: 'Olam' here describes the Philistines' long-standing ('ancient/perpetual') hostility, a human enmity of long duration, not something declared eternal.

Pr 12:19.rationale: Proverbial saying that truthful lips endure forever, contrasted with a lying tongue lasting a moment; human speech, though it could be read as a blessing on the righteous.

Mk 11:14.rationale: Jesus curses the fig tree that no one eat its fruit 'forever' (eis ton aiōna); a lasting judgment, often read as enacted judgment on the unfruitful temple, framing the cleansing.

Rev 4:9.rationale: The One seated on the throne is described as he 'who lives forever and ever', ascribing eternal life to God himself.

Rev 4:10.rationale: The elders worship 'Him who lives forever and ever', directly calling God's life eternal.

Mt 13:22.rationale: "Worries of this life" (lit. "of the age") refers to the present age, not to anything being eternal.

Mt 13:39.rationale: "End of the age" marks the close of the present era; nothing is called eternal.

Mt 13:40.rationale: "End of the age" is a temporal endpoint; the burning is not called eternal here.

Mt 13:49.rationale: "End of the age" denotes the consummation of this era; the fiery furnace is not described as everlasting here.

Ro 6:22.rationale: The outcome of being slaves to God is explicitly called "eternal life" (zōēn aiōnion), life God gives believers.

Ro 6:23.rationale: The gift of God is "eternal life in Christ Jesus," contrasted with death as sin's wages.

Heb 11:3.rationale: Here αἰῶνας means "the universe" or "worlds" (the created ages), describing creation by God's word, not calling anything eternal or everlasting.

Eze 38:8.rationale: Tamid here describes the mountains of Israel as having been long (continually) desolate in the past, a past duration, not anything called eternal or lasting forever.

Ezr 4:15.rationale: Aramaic 'alam here means 'from ancient times', describing past antiquity of the city's sedition, not eternity.

Ezr 4:19.rationale: 'From ancient times' refers to the city's historical record of revolt, mere antiquity rather than anything eternal.

Ps 83:17.rationale: "Ever ashamed and terrified" (ʿadê-ʿad, forever) is an imprecation of lasting shame on Israel's enemies, though v.16 hopes they seek God's name, softening its finality.

Isa 19:11.rationale: Qedem here means "eastern" or "ancient" kings, describing lineage or direction, not eternity; nothing is said to last forever.

Ge 8:22.rationale: God declares the natural cycles of seasons and day and night shall never cease, though bounded by 'as long as the earth endures'.

Ps 85:5.rationale: The psalmist asks whether God will be angry forever and draw out his anger to all generations, the rhetorical question the category describes.

Ro 12:2.rationale: Here aiōn means "this world/age" as something not to be conformed to; nothing is said to be eternal or lasting forever.

Eze 16:55.rationale: "Former state" (qadmah) refers to a previous condition, mere antiquity, not eternity.

Eze 16:60.rationale: God promises to establish an "everlasting covenant" (berit olam) with Jerusalem after remembering the covenant of her youth.

Ge 3:22.rationale: The tree of life would enable man to 'live forever'; though here withheld from fallen man, it speaks of God-given everlasting life, so it fits best under life.

Ge 3:24.rationale: Qedem here means 'east', a direction, not eternity.

Ps 131:3.rationale: 'Forevermore' qualifies Israel's continuing hope in the LORD, implying Israel's perpetual relation to God; it is an exhortation rather than an explicit promise, so the fit is loose.

Ex 38:13.rationale: קֵדֶם here denotes the east side of the courtyard, a mere direction, not eternity.

Ne 2:3.rationale: Nehemiah addresses Artaxerxes with the court formula "May the king live forever," a loose human use of 'forever.'

2Ti 1:9.rationale: Greek 'before eternal times' (pro chronōn aiōniōn) places God's purpose and grace before the ages, implying their eternity. However, aiōnios here modifies 'times' and may mean only 'ages'.

Da 9:24.rationale: The seventy weeks culminate in bringing in "everlasting righteousness" (tsedeq olamim), righteousness God establishes that lasts forever.

1Ti 6:12.rationale: Timothy is urged to take hold of the eternal life to which he was called.

1Ti 6:16.rationale: God alone is immortal, and eternal dominion is ascribed to him in a doxology.

1Ti 6:17.rationale: "The present age" refers to this temporal era, not eternity.

Ps 12:7.rationale: God will guard his faithful, needy people forever (le'olam); lasting security promised to the godly. Some manuscripts read 'them' (the words), which would shift the category.
Ps 12:7.note: some Hebrew mss read “them”; cf. v. 6

Mt 25:41.rationale: The cursed are sent into "the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels"—judgment on persons and spiritual beings described as eternal.

Mt 25:46.rationale: The same adjective, aiōnios, describes both the punishment of the wicked and the life given to the righteous.

Dt 31:13.rationale: "All the days you live in the land" marks the duration of human residence, not eternity; nothing is called everlasting or forever.

Ps 109:15.rationale: Tamid here means 'continually/always' within an imprecation that sins stay before the LORD; it expresses ongoing remembrance, not eternity of anything.

Ps 109:19.rationale: BSB renders tamid 'forever': the curse is wished to cling to the wicked accuser perpetually. But tamid usually means 'continually', so its inclusion is debatable.

Ps 146:6.rationale: God's faithfulness (lit. 'keeps truth forever') is said to endure forever, an attribute of God.

Ps 146:10.rationale: The LORD's reign is declared to be forever and for all generations; Zion is addressed but not itself called eternal.

Lev 7:34.rationale: The breast and thigh of peace offerings are given to Aaron and his sons as a 'permanent portion' (chok olam), a perpetual priestly due.

Lev 7:36.rationale: The priests' portion is called a 'permanent portion for the generations to come' (chuqqat olam), a perpetual statute.

Jer 3:5.rationale: Israel asks whether God will be angry forever or indignant to the end, a question about the duration of his anger.

Jer 3:12.rationale: The LORD declares, "I will not be angry forever," denying that his anger is perpetual.

Isa 26:4.rationale: The LORD is called "the Rock eternal" (tsur olamim), an eternal Rock, which ascribes everlastingness to God himself. "Forever" (adei-ad) also qualifies the believer's trust.

Job 7:16.rationale: Job says he would not live forever (le'olam); a human lament denying endless life, applied loosely to a merely human matter rather than any eternal thing.

1Co 9:25.rationale: The imperishable crown is a reward promised to believers that never decays, contrasted with perishable athletic wreaths; 'imperishable' implies lasting forever, though not the word 'eternal'.

Ps 139:5.rationale: Qedem here means 'before/in front' spatially (behind and before), not eternity.

Ps 139:24.rationale: 'The way everlasting' (derek olam) is the path of life God leads the righteous in. Some read 'ancient way' (cf. Jer 6:16), which leaves the classification uncertain.

Ps 73:12.rationale: עוֹלָם here describes the wicked as 'always carefree' (at ease perpetually), a loose description of their present ease, not a claim of lasting forever.

Ps 73:23.rationale: תָּמִיד 'always/continually' describes the psalmist's ongoing presence with God, not something called eternal or everlasting.

Ps 73:26.rationale: God is the psalmist's 'portion forever', a lasting blessing promised to the faithful believer, set against failing flesh.

Jer 52:33.rationale: Tamid here means Jehoiachin ate regularly at the king's table; it describes habitual practice for his lifetime, not anything called eternal.

Jer 52:34.rationale: A daily allowance continuing until his death is regularity within a lifetime, explicitly bounded, not a claim of perpetuity.

Ps 93:2.rationale: "You are from all eternity" (me'olam) calls God himself eternal; his throne established of old accompanies it.

Ps 93:5.rationale: Holiness adorns God's house "for length of days", i.e. perpetually; the phrase expresses lasting duration, though less explicitly than 'olam.

Ps 61:4.rationale: The psalmist asks to dwell in God's tent forever, a lasting blessing of dwelling with God.

Ps 61:6.rationale: A wish that the king's years span 'generation and generation' resembles a 'long live the king' formula, possibly with Davidic or messianic overtones.

Ps 61:7.rationale: Prayer that the (Davidic) king sit enthroned before God forever; royal court formula, often read messianically, so the categorization is debatable.

Ps 61:8.rationale: Praise to God's name offered 'for ever' (la'ad) ascribes perpetual praise owed to him.

Mal 3:4.rationale: 'Days of old' (yemei olam) refers to former times of past antiquity, not eternity; nothing is called everlasting.

Ps 103:9.rationale: Denies that God will harbor his anger forever, the exact pattern of the 'God's anger?' category.

Ps 103:17.rationale: The LORD's loving devotion is 'from everlasting to everlasting' toward those who fear him, an eternal attribute that is also a lasting blessing to the faithful.

Ps 100:5.rationale: God's loving devotion (chesed) is said to endure forever and his faithfulness to continue to all generations, both attributes of God.
